sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: school bus on your side versus the far side and undivided versus divided roads, approaching versus stopped emergency vehicles, motorcycle versus bicycle spacing, and the front versus rear truck no-zone
Confusable pairs among sharing-the-road rules, where the right action depends on which side, which road type or which road user is involved; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec11-R01 | anchor: A01
On an ordinary two-way road you stop for a flashing school bus on either side, but on a divided highway with a barrier you stop only if you are on the bus's side. [A01]
Why it matters: group school buses; confusable undivided versus divided road; difficulty medium.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-R02 | anchor: A01
The school bus stop distance is at least 20 feet, and the signal that you may go again is the red lights no longer flashing. [A01]
Why it matters: group school buses; confusable stop distance versus release signal.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-R03 | anchor: A01
A moving emergency vehicle with lights and sirens means pull over and stop, while a stopped one with flashing lights means change to a lane away from it as you pass. [A01]
Why it matters: group emergency vehicles; confusable moving versus stopped.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-R04 | anchor: A01
For a police car stopped on the roadside, the law gives two choices, move over or slow down, so that officers have room. [A01]
Why it matters: group emergency vehicles; misconception you must always change lanes.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-R05 | anchor: A01
Pulling over for an emergency vehicle means going to the side of the road, never stopping inside an intersection. [A01]
Why it matters: group emergency vehicles; misconception stop wherever you are.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-R06 | anchor: A01
Motorcycles need extra following room because, being lightweight, they can stop faster than most vehicles. [A01]
Why it matters: group motorcycles; misconception small vehicles stop slower.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-R07 | anchor: A01
On multi-lane roads you avoid both riding right beside another driver and sitting where that driver cannot see you; moving ahead or dropping back fixes both. [A01]
Why it matters: group space; prereq blind spots.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-R08 | anchor: A02
The passing gap for a bicyclist is at least three feet, and you also wait for oncoming traffic to clear before passing. [A02]
Why it matters: group bicycles; confusable passing gap versus oncoming wait.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec11-R09 | anchor: A02
The truck no-zone behind is about 200 feet, far longer than the roughly 20-foot no-zone in front. [A02]
Why it matters: group trucks; confusable rear versus front no-zone.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec11-R10 | anchor: A02
Getting out of a truck's no-zone can mean speeding up or dropping back, and passing should take you through its blind spot quickly. [A02]
Why it matters: group trucks; misconception stay alongside to be seen.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0056]
